pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 F O U N D ATI O NS
What is a cyberattack?
A deliberate attempt to compromise confidentiality, integrity, or availability.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 07 / 72
C O N C E PT D E F I N I TI O N
CYBERATTACK
An intentional action that tries to gain 
unauthorized access, manipulate information, 
disrupt a service, or otherwise harm a digital 
system.
Target
Information, users, devices, services
Method
Technical, social, or combined
Outcome
The attempt may succeed or fail
Know the definition • classify the example • identify the control.
pages.title: What is a cyberattack?

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 F O U N D ATI O NS
Why cyberattacks matter
Consequences extend beyond stolen passwords.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 08 / 72
Students
Lost account access, exposed 
identity information, fraudulent 
messages.
Organizations
Service downtime, financial 
cost, privacy obligations.
Society
Disrupted critical services, 
reduced trust, wider ripple 
effects.
pages.title: Why cyberattacks matter

pages.title: Threats, Vulnerabilities and Risk

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 T H R E A TS  &  R I S K
Core security vocabulary
These terms describe different parts of a potential incident.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 10 / 72
Asset
Something valuable: data, service, 
device, reputation.
Threat actor
A person or group able to cause 
harm.
Vulnerability
A weakness that could be exploited.
Attack vector
A route or method used to reach a 
target.
Exploit
Use of a vulnerability to produce a 
security effect.
Risk
Potential for loss from a threat and 
its consequences.
pages.title: Core security vocabulary

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 T H R E A TS  &  R I S K
How a weakness becomes an incident
Separate the existence of a weakness from exploitation and impact.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 11 / 72
I L L U S T RA TI VE  P R O C E SS
Asset
Student database
Weakness
Missing security 
update
Threat action
Attempted 
exploitation
Incident
Unauthorized access
Impact
Potential data 
exposure

pages.title: How a weakness becomes an incident

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 T H R E A TS  &  R I S K
Threat ≠ vulnerability
One is a potential cause of harm; the other is a weakness.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 12 / 72
THREAT
Example: an attacker seeks stolen student 
credentials.
It may use different techniques or targets.
VULNERABILITY
Example: reused passwords or an unpatched 
service.
A weakness may exist before any attacker 
discovers it.VS
An exploit is one way a threat may take advantage of a vulnerability.
pages.title: Threat ≠ vulnerability

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 T H R E A TS  &  R I S K
Attack surface
The more exposed interaction points, the more places security must be considered.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 13 / 72
C O N C E PT D E F I N I TI O N
ATTACK SURFACE
The collection of digital and physical points 
through which an unauthorized actor may try 
to enter, influence, or extract data from a 
system.
Devices
Laptops, phones, servers
Services
Websites, APIs, remote access
People
Accounts, decisions, credentials
Know the definition • classify the example • identify the control.
pages.title: Attack surface

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 T H R E A TS  &  R I S K
The CIA triad: what is at stake?
Most security outcomes can be related to three objectives.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 14 / 72
Confidentiality
Only authorized people see 
personal or sensitive 
information.
Integrity
Information remains accurate 
and is changed only as 
authorized.
Availability
Services and data remain 
accessible when needed.
pages.title: The CIA triad: what is at stake?

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 T H R E A TS  &  R I S K
Why do attackers attack?
Different motivations can produce similar outward symptoms.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 15 / 72
Financial gain
Fraud, extortion, account resale.
Espionage
Seeking valuable or sensitive information.
Disruption
Stopping a service or undermining operations.
Ideology
Attempting to advance a cause or draw attention.
pages.title: Why do attackers attack?

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 T H R E A TS  &  R I S K
Insider versus external threats
Trust level and location do not reliably indicate whether an action is safe.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 16 / 72
INSIDER
Employee or student with legitimate access.
Examples: accidental sharing; misuse of 
privileges; compromised internal account.
EXTERNAL
Actor outside the authorized organization.
Examples: credential theft attempt; scanning 
exposed services; traffic flooding.
VS
Both intentional and accidental behavior can create security incidents.
pages.title: Insider versus external threats

prevention.
ASSET
University account / records
WEAKNESS

THREAT ACTION
Credential-stuffing attempt
DEFENSE
Unique password + MFA
Students should justify their reasoning rather than memorize an isolated term.
pages.title: Class activity: password reuse

From deceptive software to self-spreading threats and business disruption.
pages.title: Malware and Ransomware

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Malware is a family, not one program
Malware describes software designed to harm or misuse systems.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 19 / 72
Virus
Attaches to host content and 
propagates when executed.
Worm
Can propagate across systems 
without a user repeatedly copying it.
Trojan
Disguises its malicious purpose as 
legitimate content.
Ransomware
Blocks access to systems or data to 
extort a victim.
Spyware
Secretly collects information or 
activity.
Bot
Compromised device controlled for 
attacker-selected tasks.
pages.title: Malware is a family, not one program

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Virus: depends on a host
Virus propagation typically depends on infected executable content or files.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 20 / 72
T H R E A T C O N C E PT
VIRUS
Malicious code that inserts itself into a host file 
or program and reproduces when suitable host 
content runs.
C ON C E PTUA L P A T H
Host file
Contains code
Execution
Virus runs
New host
Further infection
May modify or infect additional host files.   •   Often requires an execution or 
file-sharing pathway.   •   Antivirus, safe handling, and patching can reduce 
risk.
pages.title: Virus: depends on a host

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Worm: self-propagation matters
A worm can spread by exploiting connectivity or vulnerable services.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 21 / 72
T H R E A T C O N C E PT
WORM
A self-replicating malware category able to 
spread between systems without attaching to an 
existing file in the same way as a classic virus.
C ON C E PTUA L P A T H
Device A
Compromised
Network
Reachable hosts
Device B
Potential infection
May exploit unpatched network services.   •   Can move quickly across 
reachable systems.   •   Segmentation and updates help contain propagation.
pages.title: Worm: self-propagation matters

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Trojan: appearance creates misplaced trust
A Trojan is categorized by deception rather than self-replication.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 22 / 72
T H R E A T C O N C E PT
TROJAN
Malicious software presented as harmless or 
useful software to persuade users to install or 
run it.
C ON C E PTUA L P A T H
Fake utility
Looks useful
Install
User executes
Hidden action
Malicious behavior
May arrive through misleading downloads.   •   Can carry spyware, backdoors, 
or other functions.   •   Verify software sources and installation permissions.
pages.title: Trojan: appearance creates misplaced trust

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Virus, worm, and Trojan
Three labels describe different mechanisms.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 23 / 72
VIRUS / WORM
Virus: relies on host content.
Worm: designed to replicate across reachable 
systems.
Both describe forms of propagation.
TROJAN
Malicious function hidden behind apparently 
legitimate content.
It does not need to self-replicate.
VS
A single malicious program may combine several behaviors.
pages.title: Virus, worm, and Trojan

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Ransomware: availability and extortion
The purpose is to pressure victims by restricting access or threatening disclosure.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 24 / 72
T H R E A T C O N C E PT
RANSOMWARE
Malware associated with extortion, often 
involving encryption or disruption of data 
access; some incidents also include data theft.
C ON C E PTUA L P A T H
Intrusion
Initial foothold
Disruption
Access restricted
Recovery
Contain + restore
Can interrupt operations and learning services.   •   A ransom payment does not 
guarantee safe recovery.   •   Offline/isolated backups and response planning 
matter.
pages.title: Ransomware: availability and extortion

D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Illustrative ransomware incident chain
An attachment is one possible route; no individual step guarantees the next.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 25 / 72
I L L U S T RA TI VE  P R O C E SS
Suspicious file
Delivery attempt
User action
Content opened
Execution
Malicious activity
Impact
Data unavailable
Response
Isolate + recover
READ THE SEQUENCE Each stage represents a conceptual step; controls can interrupt the progression.
pages.title: Illustrative ransomware incident chain

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Spyware versus keylogger
Both may threaten confidentiality, but their scopes differ.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 26 / 72
SPYWARE
Broader category: software secretly gathers 
information or monitors activity.
May target browsing, system, or account data.
KEYLOGGER
A capability that records keystrokes.
May be implemented in malicious or authorized 
monitoring software.
VS
Classification depends on behavior and authorization, not only the name.
pages.title: Spyware versus keylogger

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Botnets: one operator, many devices
Compromised devices may be coordinated into a network of bots.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 27 / 72
C O N C E PTUA L N E T W OR K — N O T  O P E R ATI O NA L I N S T R U CTI O N S
CONTROL / 
COMMAND
1 Compromised PC
2 Compromised IoT
3 Compromised server
4 Compromised phone
COORDINATED ACTIONS
pages.title: Botnets: one operator, many devices

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
How malware may arrive
Recognize exposure routes without assuming every file or link is malicious.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 28 / 72
Attachments
Suspicious messages may contain malicious files.
Untrusted apps
Unofficial installers can hide harmful components.
Unpatched services
Known software weaknesses can be exploited.
Removable media
Infected content may move between devices.
pages.title: How malware may arrive

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 M A L W AR E
Defense is more than antivirus
Layer controls because no detection technology catches every threat.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 29 / 72
Prevent
Patch, restrict privileges, verify sources.
Detect
Endpoint alerts, suspicious behavior, system logs.
Contain
Isolate affected systems and limit lateral movement.
Recover
Restore from clean, tested backups.
pages.title: Defense is more than antivirus

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S E C T I O N  3
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 30 / 72
03
Social Engineering and Phishing
People, trust, and decisions become part of the attack surface.
pages.title: Social Engineering and Phishing

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S O C I A L  E N G I N E ER I NG
The human decision is the target
Social engineering influences people to share information or take risky action.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 31 / 72
C O N C E PT D E F I N I TI O N
SOCIAL ENGINEERING
Manipulating human trust, emotions, or 
expectations to cause disclosure, access, or 
actions that the person would not otherwise 
authorize.
Impersonation
Pretending to be trusted
Pressure
Urgency, fear or reward
Verification
Independent confirmation protects
Know the definition • classify the example • identify the control.
pages.title: The human decision is the target

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S O C I A L  E N G I N E ER I NG
Four persuasion triggers
Recognizing pressure creates time for verification.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 32 / 72
Urgency
“Your account will close in 10 minutes.”
Authority
“I am calling from university IT.”
Fear
“You will lose access unless you act.”
Reward
“Claim your scholarship voucher here.”
pages.title: Four persuasion triggers

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S O C I A L  E N G I N E ER I NG
Phishing: deceptive messages
The message tries to move a recipient toward an unsafe action.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 33 / 72
T H R E A T C O N C E PT
PHISHING
A deceptive communication designed to trick 
someone into revealing information, sending 
money, or taking an action that benefits the 
sender.
C ON C E PTUA L P A T H
Message
Looks authentic
Request
Click / reply
Consequence
Potential harm
May impersonate a university, bank, colleague, or service.   •   Can use email, 
websites, attachments, or linked forms.   •   Verification should occur through a 
known trusted route.
pages.title: Phishing: deceptive messages

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S O C I A L  E N G I N E ER I NG
Anatomy of a suspicious email
Examine the identity, link destination, requested action, and urgency.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 34 / 72
FICTIONAL MESSAGE · FOR CLASSROOM USE
From: “Campus IT” <alerts@support-office.invalid>
Subject: URGENT: Your university account expires today
Your account will be disabled immediately. Confirm your password using the sign-
in page linked below to avoid losing grades.
VERIFY ACCOUNT NOW
01
Unexpected deadline
02
Unverified sender
03
Password request
Do not use the example link: .invalid is reserved for nonfunctional examples.
pages.title: Anatomy of a suspicious email

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S O C I A L  E N G I N E ER I NG
Phishing comes in several forms
The target and communication channel can change.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 35 / 72
Spear phishing
A tailored message for a specific 
person or small group.
Whaling
Targeted deception aimed at senior 
leaders.
Smishing
Phishing delivered through SMS or 
chat-like messages.
Vishing
Phishing conducted through voice 
communication.
Pretexting
Inventing a story or identity to 
obtain cooperation.
Baiting
Using an attractive offer to prompt 
unsafe action.
pages.title: Phishing comes in several forms

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S O C I A L  E N G I N E ER I NG
Fake login page: a trust problem
Brand-like appearance does not establish website identity.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 36 / 72
I L L U S T RA TI VE  P R O C E SS
Unexpected link
Message received
Lookalike page
Trusted design imitated
Credential entry
User may disclose
Account risk
Possible misuse

A human-focused message can lead to application and data-level exposure.

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S O C I A L  E N G I N E ER I NG
Legitimate or suspicious?
One visual clue is rarely enough; verify the actual request.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 38 / 72
EXPECTED NOTICE
Seen inside the official portal.
No unexpected password request.
Can be confirmed with published support contacts.
SUSPICIOUS NOTICE
Unexpected link and immediate deadline.
Requests credentials outside normal workflow.
Sender and site cannot be independently verified.
VS
Use a separate, trusted communication path to check the claim.
pages.title: Legitimate or suspicious?

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S O C I A L  E N G I N E ER I NG
Phishing workshop: the student portal
A message says “Reset your password now or your grades will disappear.”
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 39 / 72
D I S C U S S  ·  9 0  S E C O N D S
What are three reasons to pause — and two safer next steps?
RED FLAG
Unsolicited urgency
RED FLAG
Threatening consequence
VERIFY
Open official portal independently
REPORT
Contact known IT support
Students should justify their reasoning rather than memorize an isolated term.
pages.title: Phishing workshop: the student portal

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 S E C T I O N  4
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 40 / 72
04
Network-Based Attacks
Availability, trust, and data flow across connected systems.
pages.title: Network-Based Attacks

pages.text:

Normal traffic: request and response
The legitimate communication path provides a reference model.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 41 / 72
Student Laptop
User
Campus Wi-Fi
Access
Firewall
Perimeter
Web Portal
Application
Student Data
Asset
Blue path: ordinary authorized request through interconnected systems.
pages.title: Normal traffic: request and response

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 N E T W O RK A T T A C KS
DoS: exhausting a service
A denial-of-service event targets availability.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 42 / 72
T H R E A T C O N C E PT
DoS
An attempt to make a service unavailable or 
degraded by overwhelming resources or 
otherwise interfering with normal operation.
C ON C E PTUA L P A T H
One source
Disruptive requests
Target
Overload or fault
User
Service unavailable
The target may be a service, link, or infrastructure component.   •   Legitimate 
users experience delay or failure.   •   Rate controls and resilient architecture 
can reduce some effects.
pages.title: DoS: exhausting a service

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 N E T W O RK A T T A C KS
DDoS: traffic from many sources
Distributed sources can create larger, harder-to-filter disruption.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 43 / 72
C O N C E PTUA L N E T W OR K — N O T  O P E R ATI O NA L I N S T R U CTI O N S
PUBLIC SERVICE
1 Source A
2 Source B
3 Source C
4 Source D
DISTRIBUTED TRAFFIC FLOOD
pages.title: DDoS: traffic from many sources

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 N E T W O RK A T T A C KS
DoS versus DDoS
The key distinction is how the disruptive activity is distributed.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 44 / 72
DoS
One source or limited origin of disruptive activity.
May exhaust bandwidth, connection capacity, or 
application resources.
DDoS
Multiple distributed sources participate.
Mitigation often relies on upstream filtering, 
capacity, and coordinated response.
VS
A large amount of traffic alone is not proof of an attack.
pages.title: DoS versus DDoS

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 N E T W O RK A T T A C KS
Man-in-the-Middle concept
An attacker attempts to observe or alter communication between parties.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 45 / 72
1
STUDENT DEVICE
!
UNTRUSTED 
INTERMEDIARY
3
WEB SERVICE
Modern TLS helps protect contents and detect tampering when correctly implemented and validated.
pages.title: Man-in-the-Middle concept

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 N E T W O RK A T T A C KS
Network sniffing and encryption
Observing traffic is not the same as reading protected content.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 46 / 72
UNPROTECTED TRAFFIC
Network observers may be able to read transmitted 
application data when the protocol lacks 
encryption.
ENCRYPTED TRAFFIC
An observer may see connection metadata, but 
correctly protected application content should 
remain confidential.
VS
Encryption protects content; endpoint trust and certificate validation still matter.
pages.title: Network sniffing and encryption

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 N E T W O RK A T T A C KS
Spoofing: misleading identity or context
Different protocols offer different types of identifiers.
CYBER ATTACKS, THREATS & VULNERABILITIES 47 / 72
IP spoofing
A packet carries a forged source IP address.
ARP spoofing
Misleading local address-mapping information.
DNS spoofing
False name-resolution information redirects a lookup.
Email spoofing
Message headers may misrepresent the sender.
pages.title: Spoofing: misleading identity or context

pages.text:
D S I 1 0 2   /   W E E K  0 9 N E T W O RK A T T A C KS
DNS: correct result or redirection?
Name resolution connects a requested service name with an IP address.

Content
Untrusted input
Page
Unsafe rendering

CSRF

request to a target application.
C ON C E PTUA L P A T H
User
Authenticated
Trigger
Unwanted request
App
Must verify intent

reauthentication.

Question: Who are you?

sign-in process.
AUTHORIZATION
Question: What may you do?
Example: a student can view only their own 
academic record.
VS
Both controls are necessary; authentication alone does not enforce data ownership.

Request
Resource + action
Policy
Check authority
Result
Allow / deny

security boundary.   •   Apply least privilege and test role boundaries.
